85.title: The hare in the moon
85.hook: a hare with nothing to give offers himself to a hungry guest; his image is set on the moon (Jataka 316)
85.howItsDone: Jataka tales like the hare's are told to children, painted on temple walls and performed as plays across Buddhist Asia, and Buddhists hear in them the perfections, such as generosity, that the Buddha is said to have practiced over many lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, parinibbana, and the last words: all things put together come apart, so keep going. Your line was strive on with care. Day eighty-five, and a new week: the Jataka, as shorts.

Tonight, if the sky is clear, look up at the moon. Some people see a face there. In stories told from India to Japan, people see a hare. We've just walked with the Buddha to the end of his life. Now the path turns to something lighter and very old: the Jataka tales, a great collection of stories that tradition says the Buddha told about his own earlier lives, as an animal, a king, a merchant, a monkey. They were painted on temple walls and carved on stone gates, and they're still told to children. The first one this week begins in a forest, with four friends: an otter, a jackal, a monkey, and a hare.
screen: `A HARE IN THE MOON.` → `THE JATAKA: EARLIER LIVES.` → `FOUR FRIENDS IN A FOREST.`

segments.voice: The hare is wise, and he teaches the others. One day he says: tomorrow is a holy day. Let's keep it well, and if anyone comes asking for food, let's give from what we have. The next morning, each goes out. The otter finds fish on a riverbank. The jackal finds some meat and a pot of curds. The monkey brings mangoes. But the hare only eats grass. And he thinks: I can't offer anyone grass. If a hungry guest comes, I'll give him my own body. Now, the king of the gods, Sakka, hears about this and decides to test it. He comes down disguised as a hungry traveler, and visits each friend in turn. The otter offers fish. The jackal offers meat. The monkey offers mangoes. Then he comes to the hare. And the hare says: gather some wood and make a fire. I'll give you something I've never given before. The fire is lit. The hare shakes himself three times, so that any tiny creatures in his fur can escape and won't be harmed. And he leaps into the flames. But the fire is cold. Not a hair on him is singed. The traveler reveals himself as Sakka. He says he came only to test him. And so that the hare's gift will be remembered, he draws the hare's image on the face of the moon, to last through this whole age of the world. Whatever anyone sees in the moon, the story's shape is plain. The hare had the least of anyone. And he gave the most, the one thing he had. Even then, he shook himself first, so he wouldn't hurt even the smallest creatures in his fur.
screen: `FOUR FRIENDS, ONE HOLY DAY.` · `THE HARE ONLY HAS GRASS.` · `HE SHAKES HIMSELF THREE TIMES.` · `DRAWN ON THE MOON.` · then, large: `GIVE WHAT YOU HAVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find what you have to give. Settle and breathe. Some days there doesn't seem to be much to give. Not much money, not much energy. Ask yourself, like the hare: what do I actually have? Time. Attention. A skill. A listening ear. A good laugh. Pick one. Picture giving it, fully, to someone who needs it. And tonight, if you can, look up for the hare in the moon. The bell holds the time.
Sasa. The hare who, with only grass to give, offered his whole self to a hungry guest, and whose image was drawn on the moon.
Your line: give what you have. Today, give one thing you actually have, time, attention, a skill, instead of waiting until you have more. Day eighty-five.

86.title: The banyan deer
86.hook: a deer king takes the place of a pregnant doe; the hunting king is moved to stop the hunt (Jataka 12)
86.howItsDone: The banyan deer story is told in Buddhist schools and temples to illustrate compassion and self-sacrifice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sasa, the hare in the moon, who had only grass and gave himself. Your line was give what you have. Did you see him last night? Day eighty-six.

Have you ever taken someone's shift so they could be at a birth, or a funeral, or just sleep? Somebody's turn was coming, and you stepped in. In the days when Brahmadatta ruled Benares, the story goes, the king loved to hunt deer, and every day he dragged the townspeople out of their fields to help. The people got tired of it. So they drove a whole forest of deer into the king's park and shut the gate, and said: there. Now hunt them there. In that park were two herds, each with its own king. One was a golden deer called Banyan. That's our hero. The other was called Branch.
screen: `TAKING SOMEONE'S SHIFT.` → `A KING WHO LOVED TO HUNT.` → `TWO HERDS IN ONE PARK.`

segments.voice: Every day the king or his cook came and shot at the deer, and many were wounded in the chaos, not just the one taken. So Banyan went to Branch and proposed a grim deal. Instead of this, let's draw lots. One deer each day goes to the chopping block on its own, and the herds take turns. Fewer will suffer. And the king, who admired the two golden deer, had already promised that he would never kill their leaders. One day the lot falls on a doe in Branch's herd who is about to give birth. She goes to her king and asks: let me have my fawn first, and then I'll go. Branch refuses. It's your turn. Go. So she goes to the other king, Banyan, and asks him. And Banyan says: go home. I'll take your turn. He walks to the block, and lays his head down on it. The cook runs to tell the king. The king comes, and says: but I spared you. Why are you here? And the deer explains about the doe. And the king is moved beyond words. He says: I have never seen such kindness, even among people. Get up. I spare your life and hers. And Banyan says: and the rest of the deer? Them too. And the other animals in the forest? Them too. And the birds? And the fish in the water? One by one, the deer king asks, until every creature has been given its safety. Tradition says this was one of the Buddha's earlier lives. The Jataka ends with a verse that boils down to this: better to stay close to Banyan than to live with Branch.
screen: `A GRIM DEAL: ONE A DAY.` · `THE DOE'S TURN COMES.` · `I'LL TAKE YOUR TURN.` · `SAFETY FOR EVERY CREATURE.` · then, large: `STAND IN FOR SOMEONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one hard turn you could take for someone today. Settle and breathe. Think of the people around you. Who's carrying something heavy right now? A new parent. A worn-out coworker. A friend with a sick relative. Picture one of them. Now picture yourself stepping in for one small thing. The dishes. The school run. A phone call they dread. You don't have to lay your head on a block. Just take one turn. The bell holds the time.
Nigrodha. The banyan deer, a golden deer king who took a pregnant doe's turn at the block, and moved a hunting king to spare every creature.
Your line: stand in for someone. Today, take one hard turn off someone else's list without being asked. Day eighty-six.

87.title: The talkative tortoise
87.hook: two geese carry a tortoise on a stick; he opens his mouth to answer the jeers and falls (Jataka 215)
87.howItsDone: The talkative tortoise is told to children in Buddhist homes and schools, and Buddhist teaching counts right speech, including knowing when not to speak, as part of the eightfold path.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nigrodha, the banyan deer, who laid his head on the block in a mother's place. Your line was stand in for someone. Whose turn did you take? Day eighty-seven.

A comeback, typed and ready. A thumb hovering over send. Someone in the comments said something smug, and the reply is right there. Hold that moment. There was once a king of Benares, the story goes, who talked too much. Nobody else could get a word in. His wise adviser, who tradition says was the Buddha in an earlier life, had been waiting for a way to tell him so without getting in trouble. And one day, a tortoise fell out of the sky and landed in the palace courtyard, split in two. The king asked how on earth that happened. And the adviser told him.
screen: `THE PERFECT COMEBACK.` → `A KING WHO TALKED TOO MUCH.` → `A TORTOISE FALLS FROM THE SKY.`

segments.voice: Up in the mountains, a tortoise lived in a lake, and two young wild geese used to come there to feed. They became friends. One day the geese said: come home with us. We live in a golden cave in the Himalayas. It's beautiful. And the tortoise said: how? I can't fly. The geese had an idea. We'll hold the two ends of a stick in our beaks. You bite down on the middle. And we'll fly you there. Just one thing. You have to keep your mouth shut the whole way. Not a word. So off they go, a goose at each end, the tortoise clamped on the middle, flying over the countryside. They pass over a village, and the children look up, and start shouting: look, look! Two geese carrying a tortoise on a stick! And the tortoise gets angry. He wants to say: if my friends want to carry me, what's it to you, you brats? He opens his mouth to say it. And he lets go of the stick. And down he falls, right into the king's courtyard. Now the adviser turns to the king and says, gently, this is what happens to people who can't hold their tongue. The Jataka says the king understood the story was about him, and from then on he spoke less. What's so good about this one is that the tortoise isn't wicked. He isn't even wrong. The kids really were being rude. He just couldn't let it go unanswered. And that one reply cost him everything. The same story is told in other Indian fable collections too, like the Panchatantra. The tortoise could be anyone with a thumb over send.
screen: `A STICK, TWO GEESE, ONE TORTOISE.` · `KEEP YOUR MOUTH SHUT.` · `HE OPENS HIS MOUTH TO ANSWER.` · `THE KING SPOKE LESS.` · then, large: `NOT EVERY WORD NEEDS SAYING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one retort go unsaid, and practice it now. Settle and breathe. Remember a moment when someone said something that stung, and you wanted to fire back. Feel the words line up, ready to go. Now, like the tortoise on the stick, keep your mouth closed. Breathe through your nose. Feel the words, and let them stay unspoken. Notice that you're still flying. The bell holds the time.
Kacchapa. The tortoise carried through the sky on a stick by two geese, who opened his mouth to answer the jeers, and fell.
Your line: not every word needs saying. Today, let one comeback go unsent, and see what happens. Day eighty-seven.

88.title: The quarrelling quails
88.hook: the quails lift the net together and fly off, until they start to bicker (Jataka 33)
88.howItsDone: The quail story is told in Buddhist communities as a lesson in harmony, and harmony in the sangha, the monastic community, is something Buddhist monastic rules work hard to protect.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kacchapa, the tortoise, who opened his mouth to answer the jeers, and fell. Your line was not every word needs saying. Which comeback did you let go? Day eighty-eight.

Any group that's ever pulled off something hard together, a band, a team, a family moving house, knows the moment it starts to go wrong. It's rarely the big challenge that breaks it. It's the small stuff. Who left the dishes. Who didn't pull their weight. This Jataka is set in a forest where many thousands of quails live under one wise leader, and the leader, in this telling, is the Buddha-to-be. A bird-catcher lived nearby. He'd imitate the quail call, and when they gathered, he'd throw his net over them, and carry them off to sell. So the wise quail made a plan.
screen: `IT'S RARELY THE BIG CHALLENGE.` → `THOUSANDS OF QUAILS, ONE LEADER.` → `A BIRD-CATCHER'S NET.`

segments.voice: When the net falls on us, the leader says, every one of you put your head through a hole in the mesh. Then all together, lift, and fly. Carry the net to a thorn bush, drop it there, and slip out from underneath. And it works. The next time the bird-catcher throws his net, thousands of little heads pop up through the mesh, and the whole net rises into the air like a sail and floats off to a thorn bush. The bird-catcher spends the evening untangling his net from the thorns, empty-handed. Day after day. His wife starts asking questions. Then one day, as the quails are landing to feed, one of them accidentally steps on another's head. Who stepped on my head? I did, sorry, I didn't mean it. But the other one won't let it go. And the argument grows. Oh, I suppose you think you're the one lifting the whole net by yourself? The wise quail sees it and knows: when quarreling starts, disaster isn't far behind. And he leads the quails who'll follow him away to another place. The bird-catcher, meanwhile, bides his time. A few days later he throws his net again, over the ones who stayed. And they're still bickering. You lift it. No, you lift it. I lifted it last time, your turn. And while they argue about who should lift, nobody lifts at all. The bird-catcher gathers the net and carries them all away. It's a story about an enemy, but the enemy isn't what beats them. The net was always there. It only closed when they stopped lifting together.
screen: `HEADS THROUGH THE MESH, AND LIFT.` · `THE NET FLOATS OFF LIKE A SAIL.` · `WHO STEPPED ON MY HEAD?` · `NOBODY LIFTS AT ALL.` · then, large: `TOGETHER WE LIFT THE NET.`

segments.voice: Settle and breathe. Today you'll cooperate on one small thing, and it starts with how you think about it. Think of a group you belong to, a family, a team, a household. Is there a small squabble going on? Who does what. Whose turn it is. Picture everyone under the same net. Now picture yourself, instead of arguing about who should lift, just lifting. Your end. No score kept. The bell holds the time.
Sammodamana. Living in harmony: the quails who together lifted the bird-catcher's net and flew free, until they started bickering about who was lifting.
Your line: together we lift the net. Today, pick up one shared job without asking whose turn it is. Day eighty-eight.

89.title: The monkey and the crocodile
89.hook: caught mid-river, the monkey says he left his heart up in the fig tree (Jataka 208)
89.howItsDone: The monkey and the crocodile is told to children in Buddhist homes and schools, appears in early Buddhist carving, and is found in the Panchatantra as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sammodamana, the quails, who lifted the net together until they started bickering. Your line was together we lift the net. What did you lift without keeping score? Day eighty-nine.

Sometimes the trouble only shows itself halfway across. The friendly stranger isn't friendly. The deal isn't a deal. And there's no way out except quick thinking. On the bank of the Ganges, the story goes, there lived a monkey, strong and clever. Tradition says it was the Buddha, in an earlier life. In the river lived a crocodile, and the crocodile's wife had been watching the monkey leap through the trees. And one day she said to her husband: I have a craving. I want to eat that monkey's heart.
screen: `HALFWAY ACROSS.` → `A MONKEY ON THE GANGES.` → `I WANT THAT MONKEY'S HEART.`

segments.voice: The crocodile swims up to the bank and calls to the monkey, all friendliness. Why do you stay on this side, eating the same old fruit? Across the river there are mango trees, jackfruit, the sweetest fruit you've ever tasted. Climb on my back, and I'll take you. The monkey thinks that sounds wonderful, and hops on. And the crocodile swims out into the middle of the river. Then he starts to sink. Water up to the monkey's knees. His chest. Hey, the monkey says, what are you doing? And the crocodile, sure he's won, tells him the truth. I'm not taking you anywhere. My wife wants your heart, and I'm going to drown you and bring it to her. Now the monkey could panic. He's in deep water with a crocodile underneath him. He can't fight. He can't swim to shore. Instead he laughs. Oh, friend, you should have said so! We monkeys don't keep our hearts inside us when we're out and about. We'd smash them to pieces, jumping from branch to branch. We hang them up in a tree for safekeeping. See that fig tree over there, with all the round fruit hanging on it? Those are our hearts. Take me back and I'll give you mine. And the crocodile, not the brightest, turns around and swims to the bank. The monkey leaps off his back, up into the fig tree, and calls down: you big fool. Did you really think anyone keeps his heart in a treetop? You're huge, but you have no wits at all. What makes this one lovely is where the monkey's strength came from. Not muscles. Not claws. A calm mind, in deep water. He stayed clear, and saw a way out that force could never find.
screen: `THE SWEETEST FRUIT ACROSS THE RIVER.` · `THE CROCODILE STARTS TO SINK.` · `MY HEART IS IN THE FIG TREE.` · `A CALM MIND IN DEEP WATER.` · then, large: `KEEP YOUR WITS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use wit instead of force once, starting with a calm mind. Settle and breathe. Think of a situation where you usually push. An argument. A negotiation. A kid who won't put their shoes on. Picture yourself in the middle of the river with it. Instead of struggling, take one slow breath, and ask: what's another way out? A joke? A question? A different door? Let an idea come. The bell holds the time.
Sumsumara. The crocodile who tricked the monkey into deep water, until the monkey stayed calm, said his heart was in the fig tree, and got away.
Your line: keep your wits. Today, when something goes wrong fast, take one breath before you react, and look for the clever way out. Day eighty-nine.

90.title: The golden goose
90.hook: a golden bird gives one feather at a time; the greedy wife plucks it bare and the gold turns ordinary (Jataka 136)
90.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the golden goose story to teach contentment (santutthi), and the Jataka's frame story ties it to a monastic rule about taking more than was offered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sumsumara, the crocodile: my heart is in the fig tree, the monkey said. Your line was keep your wits. Where did wit beat force? Day ninety.

You've probably heard of the goose that laid the golden eggs, the farmer who cut it open to get all the gold at once, and got nothing. That's Aesop. There's a cousin of it in the Jataka, and it's stranger and sadder. Long ago, the story goes, a good man died and left behind a wife and three daughters with almost nothing. He was reborn, tradition says, as a goose with feathers of pure gold, and one day he remembered his old life. He remembered the family he'd left. And he flew to find them, living poor, working for other people. So he landed on their roof.
screen: `NOT THE GOOSE WITH THE EGGS.` → `A FATHER REBORN AS A GOLDEN GOOSE.` → `HE FLIES HOME.`

segments.voice: The family is frightened at first. Then the goose tells them who he is. I was your husband, your father. I've come to help. Each time I come, I'll leave you one of my golden feathers. And he does. Every so often he visits, and drops a feather of real gold. They sell them. Little by little, the family's life gets easier. There's food. There's a little comfort. And then the mother starts thinking. Birds can't be trusted, she says to her daughters. One day he'll just stop coming. Next time, let's pluck him bare and get all the gold at once. The daughters refuse. That would hurt him, they say. But the next time the goose comes, the mother grabs him and pulls out every feather. And the gold turns ordinary. The feathers, plucked against his will, lose their shine and become plain feathers, no better than a crane's. The story says only that they were plucked against his will; some readers take the point to be that the gold was his to give, and taken by force, it was gold no more. His wings are bare. He can't fly. They put him in a big jar and feed him, and in time his feathers grow back. But they grow back plain white. And when he can fly again, he flies away, and never comes back. The verse at the end of the Jataka says something like: be content with what you're given. Greed loses even the gold you had. Notice the shape of it. It's not a punishment from outside. The gift simply couldn't survive being grabbed. One feather at a time, freely given, was more than enough. All at once, taken, was nothing.
screen: `ONE GOLDEN FEATHER AT A TIME.` · `LET'S PLUCK HIM BARE.` · `THE GOLD TURNS ORDINARY.` · `HE FLIES AWAY FOR GOOD.` · then, large: `GREED PLUCKS THE GOOSE BARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take only what you need today, and notice the pull for more. Settle and breathe. Think of something good in your life that comes a little at a time. A friendship. Rest. A person's patience. Money, maybe. Notice any part of you that wants to grab it all, now, just in case. Feel the grip. Then, on an out-breath, loosen it. One feather at a time is enough. The bell holds the time.
Hamsa. The golden goose: a father reborn as this bird, giving one feather at a time, until greed plucked him bare and the gold turned ordinary.
Your line: greed plucks the goose bare. Today, take only what you need, one plate, one purchase, one ask, and leave the rest. Day ninety.

91.title: The ruru deer
91.hook: a golden deer saves a drowning man, who later betrays him to the king
91.howItsDone: Buddhists tell Jataka stories like this one in temples, schools and at home, and Buddhist teaching holds up doing good without expecting a return as part of the perfection of giving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hamsa, the golden goose: one feather at a time, until greed pulled them all and the gold turned plain. Your line was greed plucks the goose bare. Did you take only what you needed? Day ninety-one, the last of the short stories.

Money lent and quietly never mentioned again. A favor nobody returned. A door held open, and the person walks through looking at a phone. There's a small voice that says: next time, don't bother. Today's story is for that voice. It's number 482 in the Jataka, the collection of tales about the Buddha's earlier lives. A deer with a coat like gold, a river in flood, and a man shouting for help. It's a short story about a long question: why do good for people who won't thank you?
screen: `A FAVOR NOBODY RETURNED.` → `NEXT TIME, DON'T BOTHER?` → `A RIVER IN FLOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the story. A young man from a rich family has wasted everything he had. Buried in debt, he throws himself into the Ganges. Then, in the water, he changes his mind and screams for help. On the bank lives a ruru deer, the Bodhisatta, the Buddha-to-be, with golden skin and a gentle voice. He wades into the current, lets the man grab hold, and carries him to shore. He warms him, feeds him, shows him the road home. He asks one thing: don't tell anyone where I live. The man promises. Meanwhile, in the city, the queen dreams of a golden deer teaching the law, and she asks the king to find him. The king offers a reward: a village, and a thousand coins. And the man he saved hears it and goes straight to the palace. He leads the king to the river. The king raises his bow. The deer speaks, in a human voice, and asks who showed him the way. When the king hears the whole story, he's so disgusted he wants to shoot the traitor instead. And here's the turn that makes it a Jataka. The deer steps between them and asks the king to spare the man. He's still saving him. The king lets him go, takes the deer to the city with honor, and the deer teaches the court. So what's the point? Not that people are awful. The story is honest that some are. The point is where the deer's goodness lives. It never depended on the man's gratitude. It came from the deer. The ingratitude doesn't cancel the rescue. It just shows who each of them was.
screen: `A MAN IN THE FLOOD.` · `THE DEER CARRIES HIM OUT.` · `THE MAN SELLS HIM TO THE KING.` · `THE DEER SAVES HIM AGAIN.` · then, large: `DO IT ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one good thing you did that nobody thanked you for. Notice whatever comes with it, maybe a sting, maybe a little scorekeeping. Don't push it away. Now picture the deer on the riverbank, choosing to wade in. Let the act you did stand on its own, finished and complete, whether or not anyone saw. Breathe with that. If a thought comes up about what they owe you, let it float past like a leaf on the river. The bell holds the time.
Ruru. The golden deer who saved a drowning man, was betrayed by him, and then saved him again.
Your line: do it anyway. Today, do one kind thing for someone who probably won't notice, and don't mention it. Day ninety-one.

myth: the story ends with the deer taking revenge on the man
the deer asks the king to spare him: he saves the man a second time.
the man had promised not to tell where the deer lived
the deer asked one thing in return, and the man broke it for a reward.
the story says most people are ungrateful
it's honest that some are, but its point is that the deer's goodness never depended on thanks.

fork.setup: you're the golden deer. the man who betrayed you is about to be shot by the king. what do you do?
options: ask the king to spare him.
fork.reveal: the deer steps in and asks for the man's life. the king spares him, and the deer goes on to teach the court.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: a kind of deer; the Ruru Jataka is number 482 in the Pali collection.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fable about an ungrateful man.
what it means: goodness that doesn't need thanks; the deer saves the man twice.
what a scholar hears: the same tale is retold in Aryasura's Jatakamala, a Sanskrit collection of Jataka in verse and prose.
